reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of fumarate hydratase (fumarase, FH), a tricarboxylic acid cycle enzyme that hydrates fumarate to malate, with both mitochondrial and cytosolic isoforms from one gene

The recessive biallelic disorder causes a severe neonatal/infantile encephalopathy with hypotonia, seizures, failure to thrive, and characteristic brain malformations such as polymicrogyria and an open operculum
The biochemical signature is markedly elevated urinary fumaric acid (fumarate) on organic acid analysis, often with other TCA-cycle intermediates

The same gene underlies hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC): heterozygous carriers, including parents, are predisposed to cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas and an aggressive form of renal cell carcinoma
Fumarate acts as an oncometabolite, inhibiting 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and stabilising hypoxia-inducible factor, linking the enzyme defect to tumourigenesis
Recognition of a biallelic case has implications for the wider family because of the dominant cancer-predisposition risk in carriers
Management of the severe infantile disorder is supportive; carrier relatives warrant tumour surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Fumarate hydratase catalyses the reversible hydration of fumarate to malate within the citric acid cycle, a step central to mitochondrial energy production. Biallelic loss of function impairs oxidative metabolism and causes fumarate and related intermediates to accumulate and spill into the urine as fumaric aciduria. The resulting bioenergetic failure in the developing brain produces the severe encephalopathy and cortical malformations. Accumulated fumarate also behaves as an oncometabolite: it competitively inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor, promoting tumour formation, which is why monoallelic mutation carriers are at risk of leiomyomas and renal cell carcinoma (the HLRCC syndrome).
additionalDifferentials: Other organic acidurias presenting with neonatal encephalopathy
Congenital cortical malformation syndromes (e.g. other causes of polymicrogyria)
Peroxisomal disorders with neonatal hypotonia and seizures
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids demonstrating marked fumarate elevation
Brain MRI for polymicrogyria, open operculum, and other malformations
Fumarate hydratase enzyme activity in leucocytes or fibroblasts
Molecular analysis of the FH gene
Family history and carrier assessment for HLRCC-related tumours
Renal imaging surveillance for carrier relatives
redFlags: Severe neonatal encephalopathy with seizures and brain malformation
Family history of uterine or cutaneous leiomyomas and renal cell carcinoma indicating HLRCC risk
New renal mass in a carrier relative requiring urgent evaluation
Progressive failure to thrive and neurological decline in the affected infant
reference.prognosis: The biallelic infantile disorder carries a poor prognosis with severe neurological impairment and frequent early death. The clinically important legacy for the family is the autosomal dominant HLRCC cancer risk in heterozygous carriers, for whom surveillance can be life-saving.
pitfalls: Failing to counsel the family about the dominant HLRCC cancer risk after diagnosing a biallelic case
Overlooking fumarate on organic acid analysis as a diagnostic clue
Attributing the malformation to hypoxic injury rather than a metabolic cause
Not arranging renal and dermatological surveillance for carrier relatives
references: Scriver's OMMBID: fumarase deficiency and the tricarboxylic acid cycle
Nyhan, Atlas of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: No disease-specific therapy exists for the biallelic disorder; management is supportive
Antiepileptic drugs for seizures and supportive management of the severe encephalopathy
Nutritional support with gastrostomy feeding for failure to thrive and feeding difficulties
Multidisciplinary neurodisability and palliative care given the poor prognosis
Genetic counselling for the family, recognising the autosomal dominant HLRCC cancer risk in heterozygous carriers
Surveillance of carrier relatives for renal cell carcinoma with regular renal MRI
Dermatological and gynaecological review of carriers for cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas
